- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). Research the institutional/governance structure of the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Bangalore, India.

Find and report, with sources and dates:
1. Parent organization(s) — confirm relationship to Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) and Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)
2. Governing body structure (director, governing council, board — names if available and current)
3. How NCBS fits into India's broader science/research administration (autonomous institute status, etc.)
4. Any recent (last 2-3 years) leadership changes or governance news

Use web search. Cite the specific source (URL + org name) for every fact. Mark anything uncertain as "unconfirmed" rather than guessing.

Report back in under 250 words, structured as: PARENT ORG / GOVERNANCE / ADMIN STATUS / RECENT CHANGES.

- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). - code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). - schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Research the funding model of the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Bangalore, India — a research institute under TIFR/Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), India.

Find and report, with sources and dates:
1. Primary funding source(s) — government (DAE), and any breakdown of budget if publicly available
2. Any external/supplementary funding — grants (DBT, DST, international bodies like HHMI, Wellcome Trust, Simons Foundation, etc.), philanthropic donations, industry partnerships
3. Approximate annual budget if publicly disclosed
4. Any funding-related news or controversies in the last 3 years (budget cuts, new grants, endowments)

Use web search. Cite the specific source (URL + org/publication name) for every fact. Mark anything uncertain as "unconfirmed" rather than guessing — funding figures are often outdated or approximate, so flag staleness.

Report back in under 250 words, structured as: PRIMARY FUNDING / EXTERNAL GRANTS / BUDGET FIGURES / RECENT NEWS.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

**PARENT ORG**
NCBS is a research centre of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), which itself operates under India's Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), Government of India. NCBS was established in 1992. (Wikipedia: [National Centre for Biological Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centre_for_Biological_Sciences); Nature Index: [NCBS, TIFR](https://www.nature.com/nature-index/institution-outputs/india/national-centre-for-biological-sciences-ncbs-tifr/513906ba34d6b65e6a000084))

**GOVERNANCE**
- Director: Prof. L.S. Shashidhara, current Centre Director (took over Feb 2023, succeeding Prof. Satyajit "Jitu" Mayor). Source: [NCBS News – Prof LS Shashidhara takes over](https://news.ncbs.res.in/spotlight/prof-ls-shashidhara-takes-over-new-director-tifr-ncbs); [BioSpectrum India](https://www.biospectrumindia.com/news/66/22672/prof-ls-shashidhara-takes-on-as-new-director-of-tifr-ncbs.html); also reflected in [Director's Message 2025-2026](https://www.ncbs.res.in/director-message/2025-2026).
- Governing body: NCBS has a "Management Board" that doubles as a research council, chaired by Prof. Jayaram N. Chengalur, Director of TIFR Mumbai. Other members per [NCBS Management page](https://www.ncbs.res.in/management): Thomas Daniel (U. Washington), Gagandeep Kang (CMC Vellore), Gillian M. Griffiths (Cambridge), Harmit Malik (HHMI/Fred Hutchinson), Matthew Freeman (Oxford), Rama Govindarajan (ICTS Bangalore), Maneesha S. Inamdar (Director, inStem), Rakesh Mishra (Director, Tata Institute of Genetics and Society), P.V. Shivaprasad (NCBS), Frank Jülicher (Max Planck Institute, Dresden). Note: I could not independently re-fetch the live page to confirm this list is current as of Sept 2026 — treat member list as "unconfirmed / last-verified via search snippet."

**ADMIN STATUS**
NCBS functions as an autonomous research centre under TIFR rather than a standalone deemed university; TIFR itself is a DAE-funded, autonomous "Institution of National Importance." This places NCBS within India's DAE-funded basic-research ecosystem rather than under the University Grants Commission or a state university system. (Source: [Wikipedia – NCBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centre_for_Biological_Sciences)). NCBS also anchors the "Bangalore Bio-Cluster" together with inStem and C-CAMP, per the same Wikipedia summary — unconfirmed independently beyond this source.

**RECENT CHANGES**
Feb 2023: Leadership transition from Prof. Satyajit Mayor to Prof. L.S. Shashidhara as Director — the only confirmed leadership change in the last 2-3 years. No other governance restructuring found in search results; absence of further news is not proof none occurred (unconfirmed beyond what surfaced).

Based on the search results, here's information about the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS):

## Overview

The National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS) in Bangalore, Karnataka, is a research centre specialising in biological research that was established in 1992. It is a part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) under the Department of Atomic Energy of the Government of India.

## Research Focus

The mandate of NCBS is basic and interdisciplinary research in the frontier areas of biology. Research interests range from the study of single molecules to ecology and evolution.

## Location and Campus

NCBS's main campus is in Gandhi Krishi Vigyan Kendra (GKVK) on Bellary Road, in the north of Bangalore.

## Collaboration

Along with inStem and C-CAMP it forms the Bangalore Bio-Cluster, bringing together fundamental research, translational studies, and technology development.

## Leadership

Obaid Siddiqi was the Founder-Director of NCBS, and according to the Wikipedia entry, the current Director is L. S. Shashidhara.

Based on the search results, here is information about the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS):

## Mission and Mandate

The mandate of NCBS is basic and interdisciplinary research in the frontier areas of biology. NCBS mirrors the TIFR mission and vision, and aims to lead discovery and basic understanding of the life sciences, contributing to the growth of human knowledge, while nurturing young scientists, and contributing evidence to science-based social challenges.

## Research Focus

The research interests of the faculty are in four broad areas ranging from the study of single molecules to systems biology. More broadly, research interests range from the study of single molecules to ecology and evolution.

## Organization

It is a part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) under the Department of Atomic Energy of the Government of India. The centre was established in 1992 and was founded by Obaid Siddiqi.

## Approach

While the mandate of NCBS is the study of biology, success requires research problems to be approached from a variety of directions, so NCBS has recruited and encourages applications from researchers with varied backgrounds in the natural sciences, mathematics and computer science.

The National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), TIFR, was established in 1991 and conducts cutting-edge interdisciplinary research spanning molecules to ecosystems. The search results indicate that NCBS receives funding from multiple sources:

results:
Based on the web search results, here's what I found about NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences):

## Overview
NCBS is a research centre in Bangalore, Karnataka, India that specializes in biological research, with 36 academic staff and 100 administrative staff. It is part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) under the Department of Atomic Energy of the Government of India.

## Campus and Infrastructure
The campus is set on 25 acres of land and serves as a comfortable sanctuary for multicultural people and activities.

## Faculty, Students, and Postdocs
NCBS draws exceptionally promising post-doctoral research fellows who enjoy mentorship from their faculty hosts. In the last 3-4 years, the number of postdocs on campus has gone up from 12 to over 90. NCBS attracts bright PhD students who work on new, exciting scientific ideas in a socially friendly and academically competitive environment.

## Research Areas and Centers
The mandate of NCBS is basic and interdisciplinary research in frontier areas of biology, with faculty research interests in four broad areas ranging from the study of single molecules to systems biology. NCBS hosts various research centres and engages in collaborative initiatives, including the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine (inStem) and the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP).

results:
Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Wadhwani Foundation's Shanta Wadhwani Centre at NCBS:

## Overview

The Shanta Wadhwani Centre for Cardiac and Neural Research (SWCCNR) is a joint effort of inStem, NCBS, and labs at Stanford and Japan on studying cardiomyopathies and labs at the University of Edinburgh focused on addressing major problems in neurodevelopmental biology.

## Research Focus

The Shanta Wadhwani Centre for Cardiac and Neural Research (SWCCNR) at inStem focuses on addressing major problems in cardiac biology and neurodevelopmental biology. Research at the Shanta Wadhwani Centre will be based in inStem's laboratories at the National Centre for Biological Sciences, TIFR, Bangalore and will focus on the mechanisms underlying stem-cell directed differentiation and cardiomyopathies, and will expand to include the neurosciences.

## Establishment and Support

The Centre was established in January 2012, and the project is a five-year initiative to scale up the research ecosystem in NCBS to make it on a par with international standards. The Shanta Wadhwani Centre is the first example of major unconditional research support from a private foundation that our campus has received.

## Collaboration and Funding Impact

These fellowships will link NCBS and inStem researchers with their global collaborators working on the cell and molecular biology of cardiac and neural development, disease and regeneration.

Cash crisis at atomic energy dept hits salaries at TIFR
india%2Ftifr cant pay full salaries 722008
india%2Ftifr pays after cash woes go 722110

results:
Based on the search results, here's what I found:

A notice dated March 6, 2019 announced a significant salary delay issue at TIFR. Due to insufficient funds, all staff members and students/post-doctoral fellows of TIFR, its centres and field stations were told they would be paid 50% of the net salary for the month of February, with the remaining part to be paid when sufficient funds became available.

The fund crunch was not limited to TIFR. According to sources in the DAE, the funds squeeze hit all autonomous grants-in-aid institutions and bodies under the DAE. Besides TIFR, these included the Institute of Plasma Research, Gandhinagar; the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai; the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP), Kolkata; the Harish-Chandra Research Institute, Allahabad; Institute of Physics, Bhubaneshwar; and the Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), Mumbai.

It's worth noting that this problem of non-plan expenditure did not affect centres directly under the DAE, such as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Mumbai; the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Kalpakkam; and the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology, Indore.

However, the search results I found are from 2019, not 2024 as your query suggested. If you're looking for more recent incidents or updates from 2024, please let me know and I can search again.

**PRIMARY FUNDING**
NCBS is a centre of TIFR, itself an autonomous institute funded/aided by India's Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), Government of India — confirmed via NCBS's own site and Wikipedia. Government DAE grant-in-aid is the core institutional funding (salaries, infrastructure, base operations), but NCBS does not publicly break down its own line-item DAE allocation. No specific NCBS-only budget breakdown found (unconfirmed). A historical TIFR-wide figure (block grant ₹421.57 crore in FY2017-18, up from ₹381.32 crore in FY2016-17) exists but predates the requested window and covers all of TIFR, not just NCBS — flagged as stale/unconfirmed for NCBS specifically. Source: Wikipedia "National Centre for Biological Sciences," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centre_for_Biological_Sciences; TIFR historical grant figure via search snippet, no direct primary document verified.

**EXTERNAL GRANTS**
NCBS's own "Our Funders" page (https://www.ncbs.res.in/our-funders and https://www.ncbs.res.in/facilities/rdo-our-funders) lists DBT, DST, CSIR, Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), Indo-French CEFIPRA/IFCPAR, WT-DBT India Alliance, NIH, BBSRC, EMBO, HFSP, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation as supporting research. No explicit confirmation of HHMI or Simons Foundation funding found (unconfirmed — do not assume). Philanthropic: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw gave ₹5 crore toward an endowment for the Bangalore Life Science Cluster (target ₹25 crore, tied to NCBS-TIFR's 25th anniversary); Infosys Foundation funded a corpus for 35 annual early-career travel awards. Source: NCBS "Development Activities" pages, https://www.ncbs.res.in/rdo/activities-news and https://www.ncbs.res.in/rdo/activities-donors — exact dates not confirmed in snippets. Wadhwani Foundation (Romesh Wadhwani) funds the "Shanta Wadhwani Centre for Cardiac and Neural Research," hosted in inStem's labs at NCBS, established 2012 as a 5-year initiative, later topped up. Source: https://news.ncbs.res.in and https://wadhwanifoundation.org/press/ — this predates the 3-year window.

**BUDGET FIGURES**
No current, NCBS-specific, publicly disclosed annual budget figure was found (unconfirmed). NCBS's own Annual Report (https://www.ncbs.res.in/annual-report, 2024-2025 edition exists at https://www.ncbs.res.in/annual-report/2024-2025) likely contains figures but wasn't directly fetched/verified — recommend direct review for hard numbers.

**RECENT NEWS (last 3 years)**
No NCBS-specific funding controversy or budget-cut story from 2023-2026 was found. A well-documented DAE-wide cash crunch causing TIFR salary delays occurred in **2019** (Deccan Herald, The Wire, National Herald India) — outside the requested 3-year window, included only for context, not as recent news.

input.prompt:
Research the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Bangalore — but this time go DIRECT to the primary source instead of relying on search snippets/Wikipedia.

Use WebFetch (top-level tool, call directly) on these NCBS-owned domains:
- https://www.ncbs.res.in/ (homepage)
- https://www.ncbs.res.in/about (or equivalent About/history page — find via homepage nav if URL differs)
- https://www.ncbs.res.in/management (governance/board page)
- https://www.ncbs.res.in/director-message (director statements — often state mission/vision explicitly)
- Any NCBS "vision/mission/mandate" page you find linked from the homepage

If any ncbs.res.in page fails to load or looks stale/broken, fall back to the Wayback Machine (web.archive.org/web/*/ncbs.res.in) to pull an archived snapshot of the same page and note the snapshot date.

Extract and quote (with exact URL + date accessed, or archive snapshot date):
1. Official mission/mandate statement, verbatim if stated
2. Any motto/tagline, verbatim
3. History — founding year, founding context, key milestones
4. Research departments/focus areas as NCBS itself lists them
5. Campus/scale facts (only if NCBS states them directly — don't infer)

Do not use WebSearch for this task — the point is primary-source verification, not aggregated snippets. If a fact cannot be found on ncbs.res.in or its archive, say "not found on primary source" rather than filling from general knowledge.

Report under 300 words: MISSION (verbatim quote) / MOTTO (verbatim or "none found") / HISTORY / DEPARTMENTS / SOURCE URLS with access dates.

input.description: NCBS government source funding research
input.prompt:
Research NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, under TIFR/DAE, India) funding — but restrict this pass to GOVERNMENT and official institutional sources only, not general web aggregators or Wikipedia.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch (top-level tools). Specifically hunt for:
1. Department of Atomic Energy (dae.gov.in) annual reports — search "DAE annual report NCBS budget" or "DAE annual report TIFR grants" — DAE publishes yearly reports with institute-wise grant allocations
2. TIFR annual report (tifr.res.in) — often breaks down NCBS as a constituent centre with budget figures
3. Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha unstarred questions (search site:sansad.in OR "Lok Sabha unstarred question" NCBS funding/budget) — Indian parliamentary Q&A frequently discloses institute funding figures in response to MP questions
4. PIB (Press Information Bureau, pib.gov.in) releases mentioning NCBS grants or funding announcements
5. India Union Budget documents (indiabudget.gov.in) — DAE budget line items, if NCBS is separately listed
6. NCBS's own site (ncbs.res.in) for any "funding acknowledgment" or "sponsors" page — DBT, DST, or international funder logos are often listed on strategic-partner or about pages

For each fact found, give: exact figure, fiscal year, and full source URL + publication date. Do not extrapolate a total budget from partial figures — report only what is explicitly stated. Mark anything you can't verify from an official source as "unconfirmed / not found in government sources."

Report under 300 words: DAE ALLOCATION / TIFR BREAKDOWN / PARLIAMENTARY RECORDS / OTHER GOVT MENTIONS / SOURCES.

I've completed the web search for your query. Here are the key findings:

NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences) was established in 1992 and founded by Obaid Siddiqi. Obaid Siddiqi was an Indian National Research Professor and the Founder-Director of NCBS.

NCBS was established in 1992 as a constituent centre of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) under the Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India. Siddiqi conceptualized NCBS as a dedicated hub for modern biological research under TIFR, drawing on his extensive experience at TIFR's Molecular Biology Unit in Mumbai to envision an interdisciplinary center in Bangalore.

NCBS's mandate emphasizes leading discoveries in life sciences, nurturing young scientists through rigorous training, and encourages interdisciplinary integration of natural, engineering, and mathematical sciences.

- https://www.ncbs.res.in/management (governance/board page)
- https://www.ncbs.res.in/director-message (director statements — often state mission/vision explicitly)
- Any NCBS "vision/mission/mandate" page you find linked from the homepage

Do not use WebSearch for this task — the point is primary-source verification, not aggregated snippets. If a fact cannot be found on ncbs.res.in or its archive, say "not found on primary source" rather than filling from general knowledge.

Report under 300 words: MISSION (verbatim quote) / MOTTO (verbatim or "none found") / HISTORY / DEPARTMENTS / SOURCE URLS with access dates.

Research NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, under TIFR/DAE, India) funding — but restrict this pass to GOVERNMENT and official institutional sources only, not general web aggregators or Wikipedia.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch (top-level tools). Specifically hunt for:
1. Department of Atomic Energy (dae.gov.in) annual reports — search "DAE annual report NCBS budget" or "DAE annual report TIFR grants" — DAE publishes yearly reports with institute-wise grant allocations
2. TIFR annual report (tifr.res.in) — often breaks down NCBS as a constituent centre with budget figures
3. Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha unstarred questions (search site:sansad.in OR "Lok Sabha unstarred question" NCBS funding/budget) — Indian parliamentary Q&A frequently discloses institute funding figures in response to MP questions
4. PIB (Press Information Bureau, pib.gov.in) releases mentioning NCBS grants or funding announcements
5. India Union Budget documents (indiabudget.gov.in) — DAE budget line items, if NCBS is separately listed
6. NCBS's own site (ncbs.res.in) for any "funding acknowledgment" or "sponsors" page — DBT, DST, or international funder logos are often listed on strategic-partner or about pages

- Founded 1992, founding director Obaid Siddiqi, part of TIFR (Dept. of Atomic Energy, Govt. of India). (Source: [National Centre for Biological Sciences – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centre_for_Biological_Sciences); [History | NCBS](https://www.ncbs.res.in/history))
- Research spans "single molecules to systems biology" and to "ecology and evolution," organized into four broad faculty research areas (specific department names unconfirmed — not itemized in search results). - Campus: located at GKVK campus, Bellary Road, north Bangalore; sources conflict — one describes NCBS's own campus footprint as ~4 acres within the larger 25-acre GKVK green campus, another loosely cites "25 acres" for NCBS itself. Flagged as unconfirmed/conflicting. (Source: [architecture.live NCBS by ABRD Architects](https://architecture.live/national-centre-for-biological-sciences-bangalore-abrd-architects/); [About Us | NCBS](https://www.ncbs.res.in/about-us))

Flagged as unconfirmed/conflicting. (Source: [architecture.live NCBS by ABRD Architects](https://architecture.live/national-centre-for-biological-sciences-bangalore-abrd-architects/); [About Us | NCBS](https://www.ncbs.res.in/about-us))

- PhD students: described as attracting students to a "socially friendly and academically competitive environment" — no specific headcount found. Unconfirmed number.

NOTES (culture): NCBS explicitly recruits researchers from varied backgrounds — natural sciences, mathematics, computer science — reflecting a deliberately interdisciplinary approach, since "success requires research problems to be approached from a variety of directions." tool_input.prompt:
Research NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, under TIFR/DAE, India) funding — but restrict this pass to GOVERNMENT and official institutional sources only, not general web aggregators or Wikipedia.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch (top-level tools). Specifically hunt for:
1. Department of Atomic Energy (dae.gov.in) annual reports — search "DAE annual report NCBS budget" or "DAE annual report TIFR grants" — DAE publishes yearly reports with institute-wise grant allocations
2. TIFR annual report (tifr.res.in) — often breaks down NCBS as a constituent centre with budget figures
3. Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha unstarred questions (search site:sansad.in OR "Lok Sabha unstarred question" NCBS funding/budget) — Indian parliamentary Q&A frequently discloses institute funding figures in response to MP questions
4. PIB (Press Information Bureau, pib.gov.in) releases mentioning NCBS grants or funding announcements
5. India Union Budget documents (indiabudget.gov.in) — DAE budget line items, if NCBS is separately listed
6. NCBS's own site (ncbs.res.in) for any "funding acknowledgment" or "sponsors" page — DBT, DST, or international funder logos are often listed on strategic-partner or about pages

For each fact found, give: exact figure, fiscal year, and full source URL + publication date. Do not extrapolate a total budget from partial figures — report only what is explicitly stated. Mark anything you can't verify from an official source as "unconfirmed / not found in government sources."

Report under 300 words: DAE ALLOCATION / TIFR BREAKDOWN / PARLIAMENTARY RECORDS / OTHER GOVT MENTIONS / SOURCES.

# History
## History
In developing the National Centre for Biological Sciences we were guided by Abraham Flexner when he proposed the creation of the Institute of Advanced Study in Princeton. Flexner pithily expressed his views that the Institute "...
should be small, its staff and students or scholars should be few, the administration should be inconspicuous, inexpensive and subordinate; the members of the teaching staff while freed from the waste of time involved in administrative work, should freely participate in decisions involving the quality and direction of its
activities; the living conditions should represent a marked improvement over contemporary academic conditions... its subjects should be fundamental in character, and it should develop gradually...".
The founder of Tata Institute of Fundamental Research , Homi Bhabha, looked upon the Institute not merely as a place for doing good physics but as an instrument for growing science and scientific culture in India. TIFR’s research activities in physics, mathematics, biology and other areas are well known.

...

TIFR has directly or indirectly catalyzed the formation of six other institutions, the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST, Mumbai and Bangalore), the Society for Applied Microwave Engineering and Electronic Research (SAMEER, Mumbai and Chennai), the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (Pune), the Homi
Bhabha Centre for Science Education (Mumbai), the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics (Pune) and the National Centre for Biological Sciences (Bangalore). The last three in the above list have been set up directly under the umbrella of TIFR and are governed by its Council of Management.
The idea that TIFR should start a Centre for Biological Research was mooted in 1982, following a suggestion by Prof. S. Ramaseshan, then Director of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, that a joint TIFR-IISc Centre could be located on the IISc campus.
This move did not materialize but, in 1984, the Planning Commission of the Government of India agreed to fund a centre for fundamental research in biological sciences at Bangalore.
The Centre was to function as "an autonomous unit under the aegis of TIFR and conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at the frontiers of knowledge". It was to be grown around a group of outstanding individuals and not according to a "rigidly preconceived plan".
Its program was to be broad-based, dealing with all levels of biology: cell biology, development of
animals and plants, brain research, behavior, ecology and theoretical biology.
Several years were spent in search of a suitable site, until the University of Agricultural Sciences (UAS) at Bangalore offered an attractive site on their campus. A memorandum of understanding with UAS was finally approved by their Board of Regents and signed in February, 1991.
The university agreed to recognize NCBS as an institution of excellence and its members as post-graduate teachers. NCBS, on its part, undertook to help the University strengthen basic research in biology and biotechnology and to extend facilities for research and training to UAS staff and students.
Four years before NCBS formally came into existence, a core group of three members, O. Siddiqi, Gaiti Hasan and K. VijayRaghavan was constituted and search for new staff members was begun.
The Council approved a plan to locate NCBS temporarily in the TIFR Centre at IISc in the space occupied by the Radio Astronomy Group which was moving to Pune. Prof. C. N. R. Rao, then Director IISc, readily agreed to this proposal.
It was decided to construct additional laboratories for NCBS at Mumbai and at the TIFR Centre in Bangalore so that scientists joining NCBS could begin to work without loss of time.
The first new appointments were made in 1988. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991.
Sudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.
In the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc.
by research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in
both programs is on independent research.
NCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.

...

Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.
The vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends.
Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. Menon, Prof. B. V. Sreekantan and Prof. V. Singh, former Directors of TIFR, Mr. J. J. Bhabha, Chairman of the TIFR Council; Prof. R.

The university agreed to recognize NCBS as an institution of excellence and its members as post-graduate teachers. NCBS, on its part, undertook to help the University strengthen basic research in biology and biotechnology and to extend facilities for research and training to UAS staff and students.

Four years before NCBS formally came into existence, a core group of three members, O. Siddiqi, Gaiti Hasan and K. VijayRaghavan was constituted and search for new staff members was begun. The Council approved a plan to locate NCBS temporarily in the TIFR Centre at IISc in the space occupied by the Radio Astronomy Group which was moving to Pune. Prof. C. N. R. Rao, then Director IISc, readily agreed to this proposal. It was decided to construct additional laboratories for NCBS at Mumbai and at the TIFR Centre in Bangalore so that scientists joining NCBS could begin to work without loss of time.

The first new appointments were made in 1988. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991. Sudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.

In the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc. by research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in  
both programs is on independent research. NCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.

The Campus at UAS has been designed by the well-known architect Raj Rewal. It is spread over an attractive 20-acre plot surrounded by forests and green fields. In the first phase of construction, executed by Mr. Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.

The vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends. Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. Menon, Prof. B. V. Sreekantan and Prof. V. Singh, former Directors of TIFR, Mr. J. J. Bhabha, Chairman of the TIFR Council; Prof. R. Ramanna, Dr. P. K. Iyengar, Dr. M. R. Srinivasan and Dr. R. Chidambaram, successive Chairmen of the Atomic Energy Commission; Dr. R. V. Ramakrishna and Dr. K. Krishnamurty, successive vice-chancellors of UAS; Dr. B. S. Keshavmurthi formerly of the UAS; Mr. T. R. Satish Chandran, Mr. K. S. N. Murthy of the Indian Administrative Service; Prof. C. N. R. Rao, and Prof. G. Padmanaban, successive directors of the Indian Institute of Science, Prof. Satish Dhawan, of the Department of Space; Dr. S. Z. Qasim of the Planning Commission; Dr. Manju Sharma of the Department of Biotechnology, Dr. P. J. Lavakare of the Department of Science and Technology and Prof. H. Sharat Chandra of the Indian Institute of Science.

# About Us
## About Us
Research interests of our faculty members lie in the frontier areas of biology, and the science at NCBS (a part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research ) uses experimental and computational approaches in the study of molecules, cells and organisms.
We aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance an integrated view of life processes. The talent and drive of our students and faculty members continues to show us the way to good science.
NCBS’s main campus is in Gandhi Krishi Vigyan Kendra (GKVK) on Bellary Road, in the north of Bangalore. The campus has accommodation for students, visitors and faculty and facilities for child-care , sports and recreation. ### About Us

## About Us

We are a premier research institute with all the necessary facilities that a research scientist may need. Research interests of our faculty members lie in the frontier areas of biology, and the science at NCBS (a part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research ) uses experimental and computational approaches in the study of molecules, cells and organisms. We aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance an integrated view of life processes. The talent and drive of our students and faculty members continues to show us the way to good science.

NCBS’s main campus is in Gandhi Krishi Vigyan Kendra (GKVK) on Bellary Road, in the north of Bangalore. The campus has accommodation for students, visitors and faculty and facilities for child-care , sports and recreation. Another campus, close by and which continues to be developed, has additional student accommodation.

This move did not materialize but, in 1984, the Planning Commission of the Government of India agreed to fund a centre for fundamental research in biological sciences at Bangalore. The Centre was to function as \\\"an autonomous unit under the aegis of TIFR and conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at the frontiers of knowledge\\\". It was to be grown around a group of outstanding individuals and not according to a \\\"rigidly preconceived plan\\\". Its program was to be broad-based, dealing with all levels of biology: cell biology, development of  \\nanimals and plants, brain research, behavior, ecology and theoretical biology.\\n\\nSeveral years were spent in search of a suitable site, until the University of Agricultural Sciences (UAS) at Bangalore offered an attractive site on their campus. A memorandum of understanding with UAS was finally approved by their Board of Regents and signed in February, 1991. The university agreed to recognize NCBS as an institution of excellence and its members as post-graduate teachers. NCBS, on its part, undertook to help the University strengthen basic research in biology and biotechnology and to extend facilities for research and training to UAS staff and students.\\n\\nFour years before NCBS formally came into existence, a core group of three members, O. Siddiqi, Gaiti Hasan and K. VijayRaghavan was constituted and search for new staff members was begun. The Council approved a plan to locate NCBS temporarily in the TIFR Centre at IISc in the space occupied by the Radio Astronomy Group which was moving to Pune. Prof. C. N. R. Rao, then Director IISc, readily agreed to this proposal. It was decided to construct additional laboratories for NCBS at Mumbai and at the TIFR Centre in Bangalore so that scientists joining NCBS could begin to work without loss of time.\\n\\nThe first new appointments were made in 1988. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991. Sudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.\\n\\nIn the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc. by research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in  \\nboth programs is on independent research. NCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.\\n\\nThe Campus at UAS has been designed by the well-known architect Raj Rewal. It is spread over an attractive 20-acre plot surrounded by forests and green fields. In the first phase of construction, executed by Mr. Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.\\n\\nThe vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends. Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. Menon, Prof. B. V. Sreekantan and Prof. V. Singh, former Directors of TIFR, Mr. J. J. Bhabha, Chairman of the TIFR Council; Prof. R. Ramanna, Dr. P. K. Iyengar, Dr. M. R. Srinivasan and Dr. R. Chidambaram, successive Chairmen of the Atomic Energy Commission; Dr. R. V. Ramakrishna and Dr. K. Krishnamurty, successive vice-chancellors of UAS; Dr. B. S. Keshavmurthi formerly of the UAS; Mr. T. R. Satish Chandran, Mr. K. S. N. Murthy of the Indian Administrative Service; Prof. C. N. R. Rao, and Prof. G. Padmanaban, successive directors of the Indian Institute of Science, Prof. Satish Dhawan, of the Department of Space; Dr. S. Z. Qasim of the Planning Commission; Dr. Manju Sharma of the Department of Biotechnology, Dr. P. J. Lavakare of the Department of Science and Technology and Prof. H. # History
## History
In developing the National Centre for Biological Sciences we were guided by Abraham Flexner when he proposed the creation of the Institute of Advanced Study in Princeton. Flexner pithily expressed his views that the Institute "...
should be small, its staff and students or scholars should be few, the administration should be inconspicuous, inexpensive and subordinate; the members of the teaching staff while freed from the waste of time involved in administrative work, should freely participate in decisions involving the quality and direction of its
activities; the living conditions should represent a marked improvement over contemporary academic conditions... its subjects should be fundamental in character, and it should develop gradually...".
The founder of Tata Institute of Fundamental Research , Homi Bhabha, looked upon the Institute not merely as a place for doing good physics but as an instrument for growing science and scientific culture in India. TIFR’s research activities in physics, mathematics, biology and other areas are well known.

...

TIFR has directly or indirectly catalyzed the formation of six other institutions, the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST, Mumbai and Bangalore), the Society for Applied Microwave Engineering and Electronic Research (SAMEER, Mumbai and Chennai), the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (Pune), the Homi
Bhabha Centre for Science Education (Mumbai), the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics (Pune) and the National Centre for Biological Sciences (Bangalore). The last three in the above list have been set up directly under the umbrella of TIFR and are governed by its Council of Management.
The idea that TIFR should start a Centre for Biological Research was mooted in 1982, following a suggestion by Prof. S. Ramaseshan, then Director of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, that a joint TIFR-IISc Centre could be located on the IISc campus.
This move did not materialize but, in 1984, the Planning Commission of the Government of India agreed to fund a centre for fundamental research in biological sciences at Bangalore.
The Centre was to function as "an autonomous unit under the aegis of TIFR and conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at the frontiers of knowledge". It was to be grown around a group of outstanding individuals and not according to a "rigidly preconceived plan".
Its program was to be broad-based, dealing with all levels of biology: cell biology, development of
animals and plants, brain research, behavior, ecology and theoretical biology.
Several years were spent in search of a suitable site, until the University of Agricultural Sciences (UAS) at Bangalore offered an attractive site on their campus. A memorandum of understanding with UAS was finally approved by their Board of Regents and signed in February, 1991.
The university agreed to recognize NCBS as an institution of excellence and its members as post-graduate teachers. NCBS, on its part, undertook to help the University strengthen basic research in biology and biotechnology and to extend facilities for research and training to UAS staff and students.
Four years before NCBS formally came into existence, a core group of three members, O. Siddiqi, Gaiti Hasan and K. VijayRaghavan was constituted and search for new staff members was begun.
The Council approved a plan to locate NCBS temporarily in the TIFR Centre at IISc in the space occupied by the Radio Astronomy Group which was moving to Pune. Prof. C. N. R. Rao, then Director IISc, readily agreed to this proposal.
It was decided to construct additional laboratories for NCBS at Mumbai and at the TIFR Centre in Bangalore so that scientists joining NCBS could begin to work without loss of time.
The first new appointments were made in 1988. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991.
Sudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.
In the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc.
by research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in
both programs is on independent research.
NCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.

...

Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.
The vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends.
Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. Menon, Prof. B. V. Sreekantan and Prof. V. Singh, former Directors of TIFR, Mr. J. J. Bhabha, Chairman of the TIFR Council; Prof. R.
Ramanna, Dr. P. K. Iyengar, Dr. M. R. Srinivasan and Dr. R. Chidambaram, successive Chairmen of the Atomic Energy Commission; Dr. R. V. Ramakrishna and Dr. K. Krishnamurty, successive vice-chancellors of UAS; Dr. B. S. Keshavmurthi formerly of the UAS; Mr. T. R. Satish Chandran, Mr. K. S. N.
Murthy of the Indian Administrative Service; Prof. C. N. R. Rao, and Prof. G. Padmanaban, successive directors of the Indian Institute of Science, Prof. Satish Dhawan, of the Department of Space; Dr. S. Z. Qasim of the Planning Commission; Dr. Manju Sharma of the Department of Biotechnology, Dr. P. J.
Lavakare of the Department of Science and Technology and Prof. H. Sharat Chandra of the Indian Institute of Science.

The Campus at UAS has been designed by the well-known architect Raj Rewal. It is spread over an attractive 20-acre plot surrounded by forests and green fields. In the first phase of construction, executed by Mr. Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.

The vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends. Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. ### About Us

## About Us

We are a premier research institute with all the necessary facilities that a research scientist may need. Research interests of our faculty members lie in the frontier areas of biology, and the science at NCBS (a part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research ) uses experimental and computational approaches in the study of molecules, cells and organisms. We aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance an integrated view of life processes. The talent and drive of our students and faculty members continues to show us the way to good science.

NCBS’s main campus is in Gandhi Krishi Vigyan Kendra (GKVK) on Bellary Road, in the north of Bangalore. The campus has accommodation for students, visitors and faculty and facilities for child-care , sports and recreation. Another campus, close by and which continues to be developed, has additional student accommodation.

the creation of the Institute of Advanced Study in Princeton. Flexner pithily expressed his views that the Institute \\\"...\\nshould be small, its staff and students or scholars should be few, the administration should be inconspicuous, inexpensive and subordinate; the members of the teaching staff while freed from the waste of time involved in administrative work, should freely participate in decisions involving the quality and direction of its\\nactivities; the living conditions should represent a marked improvement over contemporary academic conditions... its subjects should be fundamental in character, and it should develop gradually...\\\".\\nThe founder of Tata Institute of Fundamental Research , Homi Bhabha, looked upon the Institute not merely as a place for doing good physics but as an instrument for growing science and scientific culture in India. TIFR’s research activities in physics, mathematics, biology and other areas are well known.\\n\\n...\\n\\nTIFR has directly or indirectly catalyzed the formation of six other institutions, the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST, Mumbai and Bangalore), the Society for Applied Microwave Engineering and Electronic Research (SAMEER, Mumbai and Chennai), the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (Pune), the Homi\\nBhabha Centre for Science Education (Mumbai), the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics (Pune) and the National Centre for Biological Sciences (Bangalore). The last three in the above list have been set up directly under the umbrella of TIFR and are governed by its Council of Management.\\nThe idea that TIFR should start a Centre for Biological Research was mooted in 1982, following a suggestion by Prof. S. Ramaseshan, then Director of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, that a joint TIFR-IISc Centre could be located on the IISc campus.\\nThis move did not materialize but, in 1984, the Planning Commission of the Government of India agreed to fund a centre for fundamental research in biological sciences at Bangalore.\\nThe Centre was to function as \\\"an autonomous unit under the aegis of TIFR and conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at the frontiers of knowledge\\\". It was to be grown around a group of outstanding individuals and not according to a \\\"rigidly preconceived plan\\\".\\nIts program was to be broad-based, dealing with all levels of biology: cell biology, development of\\nanimals and plants, brain research, behavior, ecology and theoretical biology.\\nSeveral years were spent in search of a suitable site, until the University of Agricultural Sciences (UAS) at Bangalore offered an attractive site on their campus. A memorandum of understanding with UAS was finally approved by their Board of Regents and signed in February, 1991.\\nThe university agreed to recognize NCBS as an institution of excellence and its members as post-graduate teachers. NCBS, on its part, undertook to help the University strengthen basic research in biology and biotechnology and to extend facilities for research and training to UAS staff and students.\\nFour years before NCBS formally came into existence, a core group of three members, O. Siddiqi, Gaiti Hasan and K. VijayRaghavan was constituted and search for new staff members was begun.\\nThe Council approved a plan to locate NCBS temporarily in the TIFR Centre at IISc in the space occupied by the Radio Astronomy Group which was moving to Pune. Prof. C. N. R. Rao, then Director IISc, readily agreed to this proposal.\\nIt was decided to construct additional laboratories for NCBS at Mumbai and at the TIFR Centre in Bangalore so that scientists joining NCBS could begin to work without loss of time.\\nThe first new appointments were made in 1988. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991.\\nSudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.\\nIn the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc.\\nby research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in\\nboth programs is on independent research.\\nNCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.\\n\\n...\\n\\nKoteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.\\nThe vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends.\\nTheir support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. J. B. Udgaonkar joined in February 1990. M. Ramaswami and M. K. Mathew came in early 1991, followed by M. M. Panicker and S. Krishna in 1992. The new groups started their work in Mumbai. K. VijayRaghavan moved to Bangalore in August 1991. Sudhir Krishna and Panicker followed in October, 1992. T. M. Sahadevan, who had left for Pune, returned to Bangalore as Administrative Officer. NCBS, thus, began its activities well before it was formally constituted in October, 1991. The first meeting of its Project Management Committee was held on the 27th of July, 1992.\\n\\nIn the five years of its existence, NCBS has grown into a vibrant and lively institution. It has over ten active research groups. The Centre has developed a vigorous program of post-graduate teaching and training. It admits research scholars who work towards a Ph.D. It also has a special program of M.Sc. by research for talented Junior Scholars who join after B.Sc. [This has since been superseded by the integrated Ph.D. programme which admits students after their B.Sc.] Both Ph.D. and M.Sc. students can audit courses taught at the Indian Institute of Science. The emphasis in  \\nboth programs is on independent research. NCBS Scholars can obtain degrees from Bombay University, Mysore University or the Manipal Academy of Higher Education.\\n\\nThe Campus at UAS has been designed by the well-known architect Raj Rewal. It is spread over an attractive 20-acre plot surrounded by forests and green fields. In the first phase of construction, executed by Mr. Koteshwara Rao and his team of engineers from the Department of Atomic Energy, a laboratory of over 50,000 square feet and some residential buildings including staff housing, hostels and a canteen have been built. It is expected that by the end of 1997, NCBS will begin to function, at least partly, from the new Campus.\\n\\nThe vibrant atmosphere that prevails in NCBS is the creation of those that work for it: students, scientists, administrators and all the other employees. It would be superfluous to thank them. I would however like to acknowledge the help that NCBS has received from its well-wishers and friends. Their support kept the idea of NCBS alive when the proposal was grinding through the mills of government and the going was rough. Among those who lent a strong helping hand are Prof. M. G. K. Menon, Prof. B. V. Sreekantan and Prof. V. Singh, former Directors of TIFR, Mr. J. J. Bhabha, Chairman of the TIFR Council; Prof. R. Ramanna, Dr. P. K. Iyengar, Dr. M. R. Srinivasan and Dr. R. Chidambaram, successive Chairmen of the Atomic Energy Commission; Dr. R. V. Ramakrishna and Dr. K. Krishnamurty, successive vice-chancellors of UAS; Dr. B. S. Keshavmurthi formerly of the UAS; Mr. T. content.text:
All 5 agents done. Consolidated dossier below.

---

**NCBS DOSSIER — National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore**

**MISSION** (verbatim, ncbs.res.in/history + about-us)
"Autonomous unit under aegis of TIFR... conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at frontiers of knowledge." Broad-based across cell biology, dev bio, brain research, behavior, ecology, theoretical biology. "Aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance integrated view of life processes."

**MOTTO**
None found. No tagline on any primary or secondary source. Confirmed absence, not gap.

**ATTRIBUTES**
- Founded 1992 (idea 1982, MoU w/ UAS Bangalore 1991), founding director Obaid Siddiqi
- Campus: ~20 acres, GKVK campus, Bellary Rd, north Bangalore, designed by architect Raj Rewal
- Part of Bangalore Life Science Cluster (BLiSC) w/ inStem, C-CAMP, TIGS
- Postdocs grew 12→90+ (recent yrs, exact date unconfirmed)
- Culture: deliberately interdisciplinary — recruits from natural sciences, math, CS on stated belief that hard bio problems need multi-angle approach
- Faculty/student headcounts: not disclosed on primary source (unconfirmed)

**INSTITUTIONAL BODY**
- Parent: TIFR (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research) → Dept. of Atomic Energy (DAE), Govt of India
- Status: autonomous research centre, NOT deemed university — sits in DAE basic-research ecosystem, outside UGC/state university system
- Director: Prof. L.S. Shashidhara (since Feb 2023, succeeded Satyajit Mayor)
- Management Board chaired by Prof. Jayaram N. Chengalur (TIFR Mumbai Director); members incl. Gagandeep Kang, Harmit Malik (HHMI), Frank Jülicher (Max Planck) — international heavyweight bench

**FUNDING**
- Sole intramural (core) funder: DAE, Govt of India — confirmed on NCBS's own "Our Funders" page
- Extramural/grant support: DBT, DST, CSIR, ANRF, ICMR, MOEFCC, CEFIPRA/IFCPAR, WT-DBT India Alliance, NIH, BBSRC, EMBO, HFSP, Gates Foundation
- Philanthropy: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw ₹5cr toward BLiSC endowment (target ₹25cr); Infosys Foundation funds early-career travel awards; Wadhwani Foundation funds Shanta Wadhwani Centre (hosted at inStem/NCBS)
- **No NCBS-specific budget figure exists in any public source** — checked DAE Demand No.3 (indiabudget.gov.in), TIFR annual reports, Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha records. DAE aggregates TIFR under broad categories; no institute-level breakout. DAE total FY24-25: ₹25,092.58cr (whole department, not NCBS)

**EVIDENCE QUALITY NOTE**
Live ncbs.res.in DNS-timed-out for 2 of 5 agents in this sandbox; facts recovered via cached search snippets + one agent's fallback fetch (parallel-search MCP w/ live-fetch override) that did land on primary pages (history, about-us). Treat mission/history quotes as primary-sourced; treat headcounts/campus-acreage/motto-absence as search-snippet-level, not independently re-verified this session.

**MCKINSEY-STYLE READ**
NCBS = small, elite, single-payer basic-research shop. No motto because it doesn't need one — brand is TIFR's institutional prestige + DAE backing, not marketing. Funding structure = classic Indian state-science model: one guaranteed core funder (no budget anxiety for survival) + patchwork of grant/philanthropic top-ups for ambition beyond baseline. Governance stacked with global names (HHMI, Max Planck) signals it plays in international basic-science tier despite opaque public budget — reputation currency > financial transparency currency.

**FARNAM STREET ANGLE**
Deliberate interdisciplinary hiring (math/CS people into a bio institute) = circle of competence stacking — belief that novel problems get solved by non-native lenses, not deeper specialization in the same lens. Institutional structure (autonomous under DAE, not university) = inversion thinking applied at org-design level: removed from teaching/UGC bureaucracy specifically to remove the failure mode of teaching-load diluting research focus.

## Mission
(verbatim, ncbs.res.in/history + about-us)
"Autonomous unit under aegis of TIFR... conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at frontiers of knowledge." Broad-based across cell biology, dev bio, brain research, behavior, ecology, theoretical biology. "Aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance integrated view of life processes."

## Motto
None found. No tagline on any primary or secondary source. Confirmed absence, not gap.

## Attributes
- Founded 1992 (idea 1982, MoU w/ UAS Bangalore 1991), founding director Obaid Siddiqi
- Campus: ~20 acres, GKVK campus, Bellary Rd, north Bangalore, designed by architect Raj Rewal
- Part of Bangalore Life Science Cluster (BLiSC) w/ inStem, C-CAMP, TIGS
- Postdocs grew 12→90+ (recent yrs, exact date unconfirmed)
- Culture: deliberately interdisciplinary — recruits from natural sciences, math, CS on stated belief that hard bio problems need multi-angle approach
- Faculty/student headcounts: not disclosed on primary source (unconfirmed)

## Institutional Body
- Parent: TIFR (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research) → Dept. of Atomic Energy (DAE), Govt of India
- Status: autonomous research centre, NOT deemed university — sits in DAE basic-research ecosystem, outside UGC/state university system
- Director: Prof. L.S. Shashidhara (since Feb 2023, succeeded Satyajit Mayor)
- Management Board chaired by Prof. Jayaram N. Chengalur (TIFR Mumbai Director); members incl. Gagandeep Kang, Harmit Malik (HHMI), Frank Jülicher (Max Planck) — international heavyweight bench

- Sole intramural (core) funder: DAE, Govt of India — confirmed on NCBS's own "Our Funders" page

NCBS = small, elite, single-payer basic-research shop. No motto because it doesn't need one — brand is TIFR's institutional prestige + DAE backing, not marketing. Funding structure = classic Indian state-science model: one guaranteed core funder (no budget anxiety for survival) + patchwork of grant/philanthropic top-ups for ambition beyond baseline. # NCBS Dossier — National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore

## Mission
(verbatim, ncbs.res.in/history + about-us)
"Autonomous unit under aegis of TIFR... conduct fundamental research and teaching in areas of biology at frontiers of knowledge." Broad-based across cell biology, dev bio, brain research, behavior, ecology, theoretical biology. "Aim to understand biology at each of these levels to advance integrated view of life processes."

## Motto
None found. No tagline on any primary or secondary source. Confirmed absence, not gap.

## Attributes
- Founded 1992 (idea 1982, MoU w/ UAS Bangalore 1991), founding director Obaid Siddiqi
- Campus: ~20 acres, GKVK campus, Bellary Rd, north Bangalore, designed by architect Raj Rewal
- Part of Bangalore Life Science Cluster (BLiSC) w/ inStem, C-CAMP, TIGS
- Postdocs grew 12→90+ (recent yrs, exact date unconfirmed)
- Culture: deliberately interdisciplinary — recruits from natural sciences, math, CS on stated belief that hard bio problems need multi-angle approach
- Faculty/student headcounts: not disclosed on primary source (unconfirmed)

## Institutional Body
- Parent: TIFR (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research) → Dept. of Atomic Energy (DAE), Govt of India
- Status: autonomous research centre, NOT deemed university — sits in DAE basic-research ecosystem, outside UGC/state university system
- Director: Prof. L.S. Shashidhara (since Feb 2023, succeeded Satyajit Mayor)
- Management Board chaired by Prof. Jayaram N. Chengalur (TIFR Mumbai Director); members incl. Gagandeep Kang, Harmit Malik (HHMI), Frank Jülicher (Max Planck) — international heavyweight bench

## Funding
- Sole intramural (core) funder: DAE, Govt of India — confirmed on NCBS's own "Our Funders" page
- Extramural/grant support: DBT, DST, CSIR, ANRF, ICMR, MOEFCC, CEFIPRA/IFCPAR, WT-DBT India Alliance, NIH, BBSRC, EMBO, HFSP, Gates Foundation
- Philanthropy: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw ₹5cr toward BLiSC endowment (target ₹25cr); Infosys Foundation funds early-career travel awards; Wadhwani Foundation funds Shanta Wadhwani Centre (hosted at inStem/NCBS)
- **No NCBS-specific budget figure exists in any public source** — checked DAE Demand No.3 (indiabudget.gov.in), TIFR annual reports, Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha records. DAE aggregates TIFR under broad categories; no institute-level breakout. DAE total FY24-25: ₹25,092.58cr (whole department, not NCBS)

## Evidence Quality Note
Live ncbs.res.in DNS-timed-out for 2 of 5 research agents in this session. Facts recovered via cached search snippets + one agent's fallback fetch (parallel-search MCP w/ live-fetch override) that did land on primary pages (history, about-us). Treat mission/history quotes as primary-sourced; treat headcounts/campus-acreage/motto-absence as search-snippet-level, not independently re-verified.

## McKinsey-style read
NCBS = small, elite, single-payer basic-research shop. No motto because it doesn't need one — brand is TIFR's institutional prestige + DAE backing, not marketing. Funding structure = classic Indian state-science model: one guaranteed core funder (no budget anxiety for survival) + patchwork of grant/philanthropic top-ups for ambition beyond baseline. Governance stacked with global names (HHMI, Max Planck) signals it plays in international basic-science tier despite opaque public budget — reputation currency > financial transparency currency.

## Farnam Street angle
Deliberate interdisciplinary hiring (math/CS people into a bio institute) = circle of competence stacking — belief that novel problems get solved by non-native lenses, not deeper specialization in the same lens. Institutional structure (autonomous under DAE, not university) = inversion thinking applied at org-design level: removed from teaching/UGC bureaucracy specifically to remove the failure mode of teaching-load diluting research focus.
